old_entry.title: Chrono Trigger
old_entry.subtitle: Time Becomes a Map to Traverse
old_entry.summary: A fairground accident sends Crono across centuries, while combined attacks make the travelling party matter in battle.
body: Crono meets Marle at Guardia's Millennial Fair. They visit Lucca's Telepod demonstration, and a malfunction sends Marle into the past. Crono follows with her pendant. A public celebration becomes the doorway to a journey through different periods of the same planet, released by Square in 1995.

Prehistory, the medieval world and the distant future give the journey different surroundings and companions. The premise makes travelling through time a practical way of exploring a world. The collaboration brought together Dragon Quest creator Yuji Horii, Final Fantasy creators and Akira Toriyama's character designs.

In battle, action gauges fill while enemies change position. Characters can combine their special Tech abilities into joint attacks. Waiting for another party member can therefore create a different opportunity from acting immediately. The people travelling together affect both the story's company and the choices available during a fight.

The game's development team included three designers that Square dubbed the "Dream Team": Hironobu Sakaguchi, creator of Square's Final Fantasy series; Yuji Horii, creator of Enix's Dragon Quest series; and Akira Toriyama, character designer of Dragon Quest and author of the Dragon Ball manga series. In addition, Takashi Tokita co-directed the game and co-wrote the scenario, Kazuhiko Aoki produced the game, while Masato Kato wrote most of the story.

editorial_features.title: Yasunori Mitsuda: choosing the sound first
editorial_features.summary: A score needs more than melodies.
body: Mitsuda remembered beginning a Super Famicom working day by searching for sounds. Using samplers such as the Akai S-3200 and E-MU EIII, he could spend hours listening through CDs before selecting material. The process complicates an account that begins and ends with writing a melody. A note's identity depended on the sound chosen to carry it. His recollection gives that preparation time a place in the work, making the eventual soundtrack the result of selection as well as composition and the limits of its playback hardware.

For later recording work, Mitsuda wanted a demo to communicate its intended texture. He selected sounds himself even though other specialists would adjust the finished recording. A convincing demo, he believed, also helped live musicians understand the standard he sought. He treated those early sounds as part of directing a session, communicating his expectations before the musicians began playing. The demonstration carried instructions that a bare sequence of pitches could not: how parts should meet, and what kind of weight or colour their combination should have.

Chrono Trigger changed who would handle the sound effects. Mitsuda recalled asking Sakaguchi for composing work, then arguing that his former duties needed a specialist. He contacted friends from school, including Yoshitaka Hirota. Their conversations continued through the project. The celebrated score thus belongs within a rearrangement of jobs, not a clean division between an inspired composer and an anonymous technical background. Somebody still had to make the other sounds work after Mitsuda moved towards music, and the interview gives that person a name and a relationship.

Mitsuda also rejected the idea that sound programming was work he simply disliked. He credited Minoru Akao alongside himself for improving the sound of Square's Super Famicom games. In another example, a scheduling conflict shifted his proposed composing role on Breath of Fire V towards production, while Hitoshi Sakimoto wrote the score and colleagues handled sound work. Those distinctions prevent a single familiar name from swallowing the credits. Composing, preparing timbres and supervising a team can overlap without becoming the same contribution to every project.

original.old_heading: Time Becomes a Map to Traverse
original.old_body: Chrono Trigger enters this calendar through concrete design choices rather than through anniversary alone. Recognizable elements such as Dream Team, Hironobu Sakaguchi, Yuji Horii, Akira Toriyama connect collaboration across studios and disciplines with narrative structure and staging. In 1995, those choices organize rules, production and presentation into an experience the player has to read while acting. That movement from intention to play is what makes the subject historically useful: systems, characters, technology and cultural context stop behaving like separate categories and begin to reinforce one another. The chapters that follow start from specific, verifiable details and trace their consequences, asking how Chrono Trigger established its identity and which parts of that identity continued to influence the medium afterward.

old_entry.title: Resident Evil
old_entry.summary: Resident Evil is a 1996 survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation.
body: Resident Evil is a 1996 survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation. It is the first main installment in Capcom's Resident Evil series. Set in the fictional Arklay mountain region in the Midwest, players control Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine, members of the elite task force S.T.A.R.S., who must escape a mansion infested with zombies and other monsters.

Resident Evil was conceived by the producer Tokuro Fujiwara, inspired by the limitations on his 1989 horror game Sweet Home. It was directed by Shinji Mikami. It went through several redesigns, first as a Super NES game in 1993, then a fully 3D first-person PlayStation game in 1994 and finally a third-person game. Gameplay consists of action, exploration, puzzle solving and inventory management. Resident Evil established many conventions seen later in the series, and in other survival horror games, including the inventory system, save system, and use of a vitals-monitoring system instead of a health counter.

Resident Evil was praised for its graphics, gameplay, sound, and atmosphere, although it received criticism for its weak dialogue and voice acting. It was an international best-seller, and became the highest-selling PlayStation game at the time. By December 1997, it had sold about 4 million copies worldwide and had grossed more than US$200 million.

Resident Evil is often ranked as one of the greatest and most influential video games ever made. It is credited with defining the survival horror genre and with returning zombies to popular culture, leading to a renewed interest in zombie films by the 2000s. It created a franchise including video games, films, comics, novels, and other merchandise. It has been ported to Sega Saturn, Windows and Nintendo DS. Its sequel, Resident Evil 2 was released in 1998. Both the game's remake and prequel were released on GameCube in 2002.

editorial_features.title: Who controls the blind spot
editorial_features.summary: Resident Evil's teams rebuilt the conditions of fear.
body: Shinji Mikami located horror before the actual attack in a 1999 interview. A player anticipating something outside the frame could remain frightened without a monster appearing. He recalled experimenting with a first person version of Resident Evil before using fixed viewpoints to arrange blind spots through framing and cuts. This is a participant's account of a design choice, rather than a complete explanation of the hardware. The camera mattered because it controlled which information a moving player could have immediately available.

The project began with Capcom's interest in the systems of Sweet Home, Mikami recalled, but making something frightening became its governing question. He challenged familiar assumptions that enemies should simply be killed and the player should naturally be stronger. Watching horror films had made him want to act differently from their doomed characters. A game could offer that opportunity within limits. Its audience needed room to form a strategy, rather than merely press through a sequence whose outcome had already been decided.

Resident Evil 4 required another difficult negotiation. Producer Hiroyuki Kobayashi remembered an overhaul without a shared picture of the final game. Staff disagreed about what Resident Evil should be, and successive versions failed to settle the question. He credited Mikami's arrival as director with bringing the eventual direction together. The account also preserves the work around that intervention: a producer managing uncertainty and a team revising ideas. A clear final camera and rhythm should not make that production struggle disappear from view.

Protecting Ashley gave that new action another constraint. Kobayashi described the need to maintain distance, avoid leaving her behind and prevent shots from hitting her during a crowded fight. He credited programmers with making those interactions work, rather than treating the companion as an inert object. Ashley could also respond to danger behind Leon. The relationship changed what the player had to notice: surviving a group was not only about aiming at attackers, but keeping another person inside a manageable space.
story_headings: The player needs room to answer

old_entry.summary: On May 31, 1996 Domark became Eidos Interactive as part of a reorganization bringing together British publishing and development businesses.
body: On May 31, 1996 Domark became Eidos Interactive as part of a reorganization bringing together British publishing and development businesses. The new identity arrived as PlayStation and 3D were changing the market, costs and imagery of games. Eidos would become associated with Tomb Raider, Championship Manager, Deus Ex, Thief, Legacy of Kain and many other series. Its history shows the publisher as a network: financing, distributing and building brands able to cross countries and platforms, often while working with studios that possessed very strong identities of their own.

Eidos emerges from the combination of different skills: publishing, development and video technology are brought into a larger structure. The May 31, 1996 name change makes visible a transformation already underway. In the mid-1990s, producing 3D games requires growing budgets, international distribution and promotional capacity. Corporate scale therefore becomes a response to technological change. Eidos attempts to give studios a commercial network large enough to bring British projects onto consoles and global markets.

The success of Tomb Raider gives Eidos a character able to cross the boundaries of a single game. Lara Croft appears in magazines, advertising and campaigns reaching beyond traditional game audiences. The publisher uses that recognition to build an international brand while Core Design produces sequels at a rapid pace. The commercial advantage is enormous, but pressure on the series also shows the risk of the model: when a character becomes a financial pillar, corporate schedules can conflict with the time required for development.

Eidos publishes games that do not share a single formula. Thief focuses on stealth and spatial simulation, Deus Ex combines systems, dialogue and choice, while Championship Manager works through data and management. This variety shows the value of a publisher able to support different design identities. The Eidos label does not require every game to look alike. It must provide distribution and visibility to complex projects. When it works, the publishing network allows very specific ideas to reach an international audience without being reduced to one dominant genre.
